uphill/curve: Training has one goal: make the loss smaller. Here is the loss as a function of a single weight, w, which sits at three.
uphill/slope: The gradient, g, is the slope of the loss right there. It is plus two: moving w to the right makes the loss go up.
uphill/against: So to go downhill, step the other way, against the gradient. The weight moves left, and the loss drops.
uphill/left: On the other side of the valley the slope is negative, so stepping against it moves w to the right. Either way, the step goes downhill.
rule/rule: That is the whole rule. The new w is the old w, minus eta times g.
rule/eta: Eta is the learning rate: a small positive number that sets how far each step goes.
rule/steep: The step is proportional to g, so a steep slope makes a big step. Near the bottom the slope flattens, and the steps shrink on their own.
rule/vector: With many weights, they all step at once, each against its own entry of the gradient. One and minus a half become zero point eight and minus zero point four.
drop/tangent: How much does one step lower the loss? Close up, the curve is almost its tangent line, so the loss changes by about the slope times the move.
drop/formula: The move is minus eta g. Times the slope g, that is minus eta g squared. Here, minus zero point four, and the true change is minus zero point three eight.
drop/always: g squared is never negative, so a small enough step never makes the loss worse. With many weights, each one adds its own minus eta g squared.
example/ask: Your turn to follow along. A weight sits at two, its gradient is three, and the learning rate is zero point one. Where does one step take it?
example/step: The step is eta times g: zero point one times three is zero point three.
example/sub: Subtract it from w: two minus zero point three is one point seven.
example/result: The gradient was positive, so the weight went down.
